final_task_tree.title: Figure out a training plan for my dog
final_task_tree.description:
Rescue border collie mix, 14 months. Pulls hard on the leash and barks at every other dog on walks. South Bay, California; I can do evenings and weekends.

Three things only:
1. Whether to hire a trainer or do it myself.
2. If hiring — two or three local options with real prices.
3. A week-by-week plan for the first four weeks.

Don't research anything beyond those three.

comments.body:
Done — report attached, tree built out. Stayed inside the three things you asked for and didn't wander.

**1. Hire or DIY → hybrid.** DIY the daily work, buy 2–3 sessions up front. At 14 months the behaviour isn't deeply rehearsed yet and border collie mixes are very trainable, so the protocols will work. But two things you can't self-supply: a calibrated read on his threshold distance (the distance where he notices a dog but can still eat), and a calm decoy dog to practise against. Don't buy a big package before someone has met him. Ruled out board-and-train — the handler skills are what need training.

**One thing to flag:** the answer partly depends on something I can't determine from here. Frustrated greeter (wiggly, whining, pulls *toward* dogs, fine once he meets them) is very DIY-able. Fear-based (stiff, hackles, growling, won't take food, reacts at 100+ ft) means hire a proper behaviour consultant, not a general trainer. There's a scoring table in the report and it's the Week 0 task. Worth doing before you spend money.

**2. Three options, real published prices:**
- **HSSV "Top Dogs Level 1"** — $300, six weeks, purpose-built for leash reactivity. Best value.
- **In Tune / Nancy Le** — $195–325 consult, $130–215 follow-ups. Strongest credential (CTC, Academy for Dog Trainers). Tiered pricing under $115K household.
- **D For Dogz "Growly Dog"** — $595 for 9 sessions over 5 weeks, Sat 9:30am + Wed 6:30pm. Best schedule fit.

Recommended combo is HSSV + one In Tune consult, ~$500–625. For contrast, D For Dogz private coaching is $2,400 — I'd skip it for a dog with no bite history.

⏰ **Time-sensitive:** the HSSV cohort starts **Wed 19 Aug at 6:15pm**, about two weeks out. If you want it, register soon.

**3. Four-week plan** — five subtasks, Week 0 through Week 4. Week 0 is gear + diagnosis, Week 1 stops him rehearsing the behaviour at all, Week 2 starts counter-conditioning at distance, Week 3 closes distance, Week 4 uses a borrowed calm dog and reviews against baseline. Two 10-minute evening sessions plus a weekend setup — fits your availability. It runs identically whether or not you hire anyone, so you can start Monday without deciding first.

**Two open items I couldn't close:**
- Nancy Le's evening/weekend availability. An older version of her site said Thursdays and Fridays only; the current site doesn't say. No phone published, so it needs an email. Flagged in that subtask.
- Whether the HSSV adopter discount applies to a dog adopted elsewhere. Worth asking.

Next moves are four subtasks: decide (15 min), register with HSSV, email Nancy, buy the kit. Phone numbers and links are in each description. Setting this to needs_review — the decision on which option is genuinely yours.

report.markdown:
_14-month rescue border collie mix · pulls hard on leash, barks at other dogs · South Bay CA · evenings and weekends_ ## The short answer **Do it yourself, but buy two or three sessions of professional help up front.** Don't buy a big package before someone has met your dog. The daily work — ten minutes an evening on your own street — is the thing that actually changes the behaviour, and no trainer can do it for you. What you're buying from a professional is two things you genuinely can't self-supply: a calibrated eye on your dog's *threshold distance*, and access to a calm decoy dog to practise against. **Recommended spend: ~$500–625.** HSSV's reactive-dog class ($300) plus one private consult ($195–325). Compare with $2,400+ for a full private package. --- ## 1. Hire or DIY? ### Why DIY is viable here - **14 months is the good news.** The behaviour is recent and not yet deeply rehearsed. This is the easiest it will ever be to change. - **Border collie mixes are highly trainable** and food/work motivated. The drive works for you once channelled. - **These are the two most-documented problems in dog training.** The protocols are public, well-tested, and free. - **The bottleneck is your consistency, not your knowledge.** That stays yours whoever you hire. ### Why buy a few sessions anyway - **Threshold distance is the hard skill.** The distance at which your dog notices another dog but can still eat and respond to you. Misjudging it is the single most common reason home efforts stall. An experienced eye fixes this in one session. - **You need a decoy dog.** A calm, neutral stooge dog at a controlled distance. Structured sessions need a helper with a calm, well-mannered, non-reactive dog on leash — you can't manufacture that on a normal walk. - **The stall signal.** Bring in a professional if progress stalls, if reactivity worsens despite consistent work, or if you aren't confident you're reading your dog correctly. ### The one thing that changes this answer Leash reactivity has two different engines, and they need different responses. A dog may be "reacting to avoid" — trying to create distance from something it perceives as a threat — or "reacting to get closer", where excitement at something it can't reach escalates into agitated barking and pulling because it's held back by the leash. | | Frustrated greeter | Fear / defensive | |---|---|---| | **Body** | Loose, wiggly; tail high and fast | Stiff; hackles up; weight back | | **Sound** | Barking with whining mixed in | Growling; air-snapping | | **Direction** | Pulls **toward** the dog | Pulls **away**, or freezes then explodes | | **Distance triggered** | Fairly close | Long range, 100+ ft | | **Food** | Will still take treats | Won't take food at all | | **Recovery** | Seconds | Minutes | | **Verdict** | **Very DIY-able.** One or two sessions is plenty | **Hire properly.** CDBC/CBCC-KA behaviour consultant | **Your first job is scoring this.** Log every dog sighting for a week — distance, body language, recovery time, whether he'd eat. That's Week 0 in the plan. ### One hard rule, whoever does the training No prong, choke, or e-collars for this problem. A dog may stop barking and lunging because of the pain, but the risk that he associates that pain with the presence of the other dog is significant, and his reaction toward other dogs may worsen through pain, fear and anxiety. Screen for this before you pay anyone. **Ruled out: board-and-train.** The handler skills are what need training. Sending the dog away trains the wrong species. --- ## 2. Three local options, real prices | | **A. HSSV Top Dogs L1** | **B. In Tune (Nancy Le)** | **C. D For Dogz Growly Dog** | |---|---|---|---| | **Price** | **$300** / 6 weeks | **$195–325** consult
$130–215 follow-ups | **$595** / 9 sessions, 5 weeks | | **Format** | Online Zoom | In-home 1:1 | In-person + Zoom | | **Schedule** | Wed 6:15pm, **starts 19 Aug 2026** | To be confirmed | Sat 9:30am + Wed 6:30pm | | **Where** | Milpitas (online) | 15 mi of Cambrian, San Jose | Palo Alto | | **Contact** | (408) 262-2133
dogtraining@hssv.org | Nancy@Intunedogtraining.com | 650-538-3011 | | **Best for** | Value; purpose-built | Credentials; calibration | Schedule fit | ### A. Humane Society Silicon Valley — "Top Dogs Level 1" · $300 · **best value** Designed specifically for dogs struggling with reactivity, online for dogs 8 months and older with no prior bite history. It covers threshold work, impulse control, calm exits and real-life coping skills, focused on reducing stress and helping you navigate everyday situations. Six weeks, one session per week — the first 90 minutes, then five sessions of 50 minutes — for dogs who bark, lunge or worry but have not caused injury. That last line is your dog exactly. **Next cohort starts Wed 19 Aug at 6:15pm** — about two weeks out, so this is the time-sensitive item. The progression matters: Level 2 is in-person, where you and your reactive dog work in a controlled group setting with real-time coaching, covering impulse control, threshold management, coping skills and emergency exits — also $300. That's where the decoy-dog work happens. Level 3 runs topics like rally and urban parkour, continuing counter-conditioning through a sport so the dog finishes more relaxed around other dogs generally — a strong fit for a herding breed that needs a job. *Caveat:* Level 1 being online means nobody watches your handling for six weeks. Pair it with one private session, or accept the delay. *Free either way:* [HSSV Reactive Dog Training Guide (PDF)](https://www.hssv.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Reactive-Dog-Training-Guide-7.11.25.pdf) ### B. In Tune Dog Training, Nancy Le · $195–325 · **strongest credential** CTC from the Academy for Dog Trainers (Jean Donaldson's programme — among the most rigorous in the field), plus SAPT and CSAT. She provides positive-reinforcement training in San Jose and nearby South Bay communities, working with puppies, adolescents and adult dogs on fear, reactivity, aggression and separation anxiety. All training is reward-based, without corrections, shock, choke or prongs. Initial consultation $195–$325, follow-ups $130–$215; she recommends starting with six sessions about twice a month, then reassessing. Tiered pricing is available for households earning under $115K a year. **Use her for one thing:** an in-person consult where she watches you walk your dog on your street and calibrates the threshold. That's the highest-leverage $200 in this whole report. *Open question:* evening/weekend availability needs confirming — an earlier version of her site listed consults on Thursdays and Fridays only. ### C. D For Dogz, "Leash Reactive Dog Foundations" · $595 · **best schedule fit** Tuition is $595 for 9 sessions completed over 5 weeks, with in-person classroom sessions Saturdays 9:30–10:30 AM and a live Zoom Q&A Wednesdays 6:30–7:15 PM. Saturday morning plus Wednesday evening is an exact match for your availability. Two design details worth noting: the first two in-person sessions are people-only, so you learn the concepts and handling skills without adding pressure on your dog, and the final session is a guided neighbourhood walk to bridge into real environments. The class focuses on teaching dogs how to disengage from triggers and re-orient back to their handler. **Skip the premium tiers** unless the class fails: Private Coaching runs $2,400 for 6 weeks and Day Training $4,200 for 6 weeks. Hard to justify for a 14-month-old with no bite history. Entry point is a free 15-minute call. *Caveat:* Palo Alto, 9:30 AM, every Saturday for five weeks. Check the drive honestly. ### Screening questions — ask before you pay anyone 1. *"What equipment will you have me use?"* — front-clip harness, head halter, long line are fine. Any mention of prong, choke, e-collar, or "corrections": walk away. 2. *"What happens if my dog reacts in your class?"* — should involve distance, barriers, calm exit. Not a correction. 3. *"How do you find my dog's threshold distance?"* 4. *"Do you use a decoy dog, and is it the same one each time?"* 5. *"What are your credentials?"* — CPDT-KA, CTC, CBCC-KA, CDBC, KPA-CTP. --- ## 3. The four-week plan Two 5–10 minute sessions on weekday evenings, plus one or two longer setup sessions at the weekend. Frequency beats duration; short and successful beats long and frustrating. ### Week 0 — this weekend **Buy:** Y-front harness with front *and* top clip; a standard 6-foot leash, which gives freedom while keeping the relaxed "J" shape — avoid retractables, which create constant tension and reinforce pulling; a 15–30 ft long line; waist treat pouch; high-value treats (chicken, cheese, hot dog, freeze-dried liver) cut to pea size; a clicker or a chosen marker word. **Diagnose:** log every dog sighting this week — distance first noticed, distance he started barking, body language, recovery time, whether he'd eat. Score it against the frustration-vs-fear table above. ### Week 1 — stop the rehearsal Every walk where he barks is a rep that strengthens the habit. This week you stop the practice, you don't fix anything yet. - **Management:** low-traffic times and routes. Avoid the trigger by ducking behind a car or tree, crossing the street, or teaching a 180 turn and walking the opposite way. Target for the week: zero barking episodes. - **Charge the marker** — say "yes!", feed. 20 reps, indoors. - **Emergency U-turn** — cue, turn, jog 3–4 steps, mark, feed. Your escape hatch for years. - **"Find it"** — toss a treat, name it. Sniffing resets an aroused dog. - **Loose leash, indoors only.** Reward the loose leash; pulling must never get your dog what they want or take them where they want to go — only mark, treat and allow movement when the leash is loose. Click and treat every one or two steps as long as he isn't pulling, and make the criteria very clear — reward for no tension, and don't allow "a little bit" of pulling, because it's too difficult for a dog to learn the difference between pulling a little and pulling a lot. The leash clip hanging straight down is a good sign the leash is loose. **Border collie note:** add 15 min/day of nosework or puzzle feeding. An under-stimulated herding dog is a more reactive dog. ### Week 2 — outside, and first counter-conditioning Take loose-leash walking to the driveway, then 20 metres, then the end of the street. **Separate your walks.** A *training walk* is 15 minutes, front clip, high treat rate, almost no distance covered. A *sniffing walk* is the long line in open space. Don't mix them. **Engage–Disengage, Level 1** — reward for *looking*. The moment your dog looks at the trigger, click or say "yes!", then immediately treat, encouraging him to turn his head toward you. Keep playing Level 1 until he has calmly engaged the trigger from every direction, especially if the trigger is moving. **The threshold rule — the most important line in this report:** the right distance is where he notices the other dog but can still eat and still respond. Don't wait for him to react — you're teaching him to associate other dogs with something wonderful. If he barks and lunges, you went too far too fast: add more distance and repeat. *If he's already staring before you can mark:* as soon as he notices the other dog but before he can overreact, feed treat after treat smoothly and quickly, 10 to 15 in a row, praising calmly. Pure association-building; requires nothing from him. ### Week 3 — Level 2, and closing distance **Engage–Disengage, Level 2** — reward for *looking away*, starting at the same distance that worked for Level 1. Let him notice the trigger, then wait 3–5 seconds to see if he offers to look away on his own; if he fixates longer than 5 seconds, go back to Level 1. The precise moment he disengages, click, then feed — and if he reacts or doesn't turn back to you after the click, move further away and reset at an easier distance. **Closing distance:** change one variable at a time — distance, *or* the other dog's movement, *or* environment. Never two. When he looks up at you for more, go closer and repeat. Expect bad days; a dog who was brilliant on Tuesday can fall apart on Thursday. **Don't let him greet dogs on leash as a reward.** Exercise caution with on-leash greetings, as frustration buildup might lead to a scuffle or altercation. ### Week 4 — decoy dog, then review Recruit a friend with a calm, non-reactive dog. Start well beyond threshold in open space. Run Level 2 with the decoy standing still, then walking slowly parallel, then gradually closer — one variable at a time. You can also use the dog's desired outcome — moving away from what's bothering him — as the reinforcer to teach an alternative behaviour. He looks calmly, you mark, you walk away. Relief becomes the payment. Powerful for a fear-based dog. **Measure against Week 0:** at what distance does he now first bark? Can he eat closer than before? How fast does he recover? Reactions per walk? Progress is measured in metres of threshold and seconds of recovery — not in the dog being "cured." **Decision point:** | Outcome | Do this | |---|---| | Clear improvement | Continue 4–8 more weeks. Add an in-person class. | | Flat or worse | Book a professional now. Stop self-directing. | | Growling / snapping / bite attempt | Get a CDBC or CBCC-KA behaviour consultant. Act early — most reactive-dog classes exclude dogs with a bite history. | --- ## Your next four moves 1. **Decide** which option (15 min) — everything waits on this 2. **Register for HSSV** if choosing A — cohort starts 19 Aug, ~2 weeks out 3. **Email Nancy Le** if choosing B — confirm evening/weekend availability 4. **Buy the kit** this weekend — needed regardless Each is a subtask with the contact details already in it.

subtasks.title: Decide: hire a trainer vs. DIY for leash pulling + dog reactivity
subtasks.description:
RECOMMENDATION: Hybrid — do the daily work yourself, but buy 2–3 private sessions with a reactivity-experienced trainer up front. Do not buy a big package before a first session.

WHY DIY IS VIABLE HERE:
- 14 months is adolescence. The behaviour is recent and not yet deeply rehearsed. This is the easiest it will ever be to change.
- Border collie mixes are highly trainable and food/work motivated. High drive works in your favour once it's channelled.
- Both problems (pulling, barking at dogs) are the two most-documented issues in dog training. The protocols are public and reliable.
- The work itself is daily 10-minute reps on your own walks. A trainer cannot do those for you — that's the actual bottleneck, and it's yours either way.

WHY BUY A FEW SESSIONS ANYWAY:
- The single hardest skill is reading your dog's threshold — the distance at which he notices another dog but can still eat and respond. Getting this wrong is why home efforts stall. An experienced eye fixes it in one session.
- Reactivity work needs a decoy dog (a calm, neutral stooge dog at a controlled distance). You can't manufacture that on a normal walk; trainers and reactive-dog classes have them.
- Sniffspot's guidance: if progress stalls, if reactivity worsens despite consistent work, or if you're not confident you're reading your dog correctly, bring in a professional.

THE FORK THAT CHANGES THE ANSWER — frustration vs fear:
Per SF SPCA, leash reactivity develops two ways: "reacting to get closer" (frustrated greeter — wants to meet, blocked by leash, escalates) or "reacting to avoid" (fear — trying to create distance from something perceived as a threat).
- FRUSTRATED GREETER signals: loose wiggly body, tail high and wagging fast, whining mixed with barking, fine with dogs once he actually meets them, pulls TOWARD the dog. → Very DIY-able. Frustration tolerance + impulse control. 2 sessions is plenty.
- FEAR / DEFENSIVE signals: hackles up, stiff body, growling, air-snapping, weight shifted backwards, reacting at very long distances (100+ ft), can't take food when he sees a dog, takes many minutes to recover after. → Hire properly. Get a CDBC/CBCC-KA behaviour consultant, not a general obedience trainer. If there's any bite history or he can't recover at all, add a veterinary behaviourist.
Watch him for a week and score this — it's the first task in the week-by-week plan.

HARD RULE ON METHOD (applies whoever does the training):
Do not use choke, prong or e-collars for this. SF SPCA: the dog may stop barking due to pain, but the risk that he associates the pain with the presence of the other dog is significant, and reactivity can worsen through fear and anxiety. Screen any trainer for this — see the screening questions in the trainer subtask.

BUDGET SHAPE: hybrid runs roughly $300–$700 all-in (1 assessment + 1–2 follow-ups, or a 6-week reactive-dog class) vs $1,500–$3,000+ for a full private package or board-and-train. Board-and-train is a poor fit specifically because the handler skills are the thing being trained.

subtasks.title: Find South Bay trainers who handle leash reactivity, with real prices
subtasks.description:
DONE — three options found, all with published prices, full details in the three child subtasks.

QUICK COMPARISON:
| Option | Price | Format | Schedule | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A. HSSV Top Dogs L1 | $300 / 6 wks | Online Zoom | Wed 6:15pm, starts 19 Aug 2026 | Best value; purpose-built for reactivity |
| B. In Tune (Nancy Le) | $195–325 consult, $130–215 follow-ups | In-home / in-person 1:1 | TBC — must confirm | Strongest credential; personal threshold calibration |
| C. D For Dogz Growly Dog | $595 / 9 sessions over 5 wks | In-person + Zoom | Sat 9:30am + Wed 6:30pm | Best schedule fit; people-only first sessions |

RECOMMENDED COMBINATION: HSSV Top Dogs Level 1 ($300) + one In Tune private consult ($195–325) = roughly $500–625. The class gives structure and curriculum; the private session gives someone watching your actual handling on your actual street. Then HSSV Level 2 in person ($300) if you want to keep going.

SCREENING QUESTIONS — ask any trainer before paying:
1. "What equipment will you have me use?" Correct answers: front-clip harness, head halter, long line. Any mention of prong, choke, e-collar or "corrections" — walk away. This is not a style preference; per SF SPCA, aversives risk the dog associating the pain with the presence of other dogs and can worsen reactivity through fear.
2. "What happens if my dog reacts in your class?" Good answer involves distance, visual barriers, and a calm exit — not a correction.
3. "How do you find my dog's threshold distance?" They should talk about the distance at which he notices a dog but can still eat and respond.
4. "Do you use a decoy/neutral dog, and is it the same dog each time?"
5. "What are your credentials?" Look for CPDT-KA, CTC, CBCC-KA, CDBC, KPA-CTP.
6. "What's your refund/cancellation policy?"

RULED OUT: board-and-train. The handler skills are the thing that actually needs training, and sending the dog away trains the wrong species.

subtasks.title: OPTION A — HSSV "Top Dogs Level 1" reactive dog course, $300 (best value)
subtasks.description:
Humane Society Silicon Valley, 901 Ames Ave, Milpitas CA 95035. Phone (408) 262-2133. Training dept email: dogtraining@hssv.org

WHAT IT IS: "Top Dogs Level 1 (Reactive Dogs)" — a six-week course built specifically for dogs struggling with leash or barrier reactivity. Covers threshold work, impulse control, calm exits, and real-life coping skills using science-based positive reinforcement.

PRICE: $300 general registration. Adopters get a discount on HSSV classes — ask, since the dog is a rescue (worth asking even if adopted elsewhere).

FORMAT: All online via Zoom (deliberate — they use online format for safety and control). First session 90 min, then 5 sessions of 50 min.

NEXT COHORT: Wed 19 Aug 2026, 6:15pm. Registration: https://pro.gofundme.com/event/e826622

ELIGIBILITY: dogs 8 months and older (fine at 14 months), no prior bite history on dogs or people. Explicitly for dogs who bark, lunge, or worry but have not caused injury — matches this dog.

THE PROGRESSION: Level 2 is the IN-PERSON follow-on, six weeks, one 50-min session/week, $300. Real-time coaching in a controlled group setting with other dogs — this is where the actual decoy-dog exposure work happens. Level 1 is the prerequisite. Level 3 is topic courses (rally, urban parkour, tricks) that keep counter-conditioning going through a sport — a genuinely good fit for a border collie mix who needs a job.

WHY IT'S THE PICK: cheapest by a wide margin, purpose-built for exactly this problem, evening start time, staffed by CPDT-KA certified trainers, and Level 2 gives you the in-person piece that online alone can't. Total for L1+L2 = $600.

CAVEAT: Level 1 being online means no hands-on eye on your handling for the first six weeks. If you want a professional watching you handle the dog sooner, pair it with a single private session (Option B) or go Option C.

FREE REGARDLESS: HSSV publishes a Reactive Dog Training Guide PDF at https://www.hssv.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Reactive-Dog-Training-Guide-7.11.25.pdf — download it whether or not you enrol.

subtasks.title: OPTION B — In Tune Dog Training (Nancy Le), $195–$325 first session

Nancy Le, In Tune Dog Training, San Jose. Email: Nancy@Intunedogtraining.com. Site: https://www.intunedogtraining.com | Booking: https://www.intunedogtraining.com/book

CREDENTIALS (the strongest of the three): CTC — Academy for Dog Trainers, Jean Donaldson's program, one of the most rigorous credentials in the field. Also SAPT and CSAT. PRICE (from her FAQ): Initial consultation $195–$325. Follow-ups $130–$215. She recommends starting with 6 sessions, meeting about twice a month, then reassessing. So a realistic full course is roughly $1,000–$1,400 — but you can buy just the initial consult.

TIERED PRICING: reduced rates for households earning under $115K/year. Details: https://www.intunedogtraining.com/booktier

SERVICE AREA: primarily within 15 miles of the Cambrian neighbourhood, San Jose. Covers Campbell, Sunnyvale, Cupertino, Santa Clara, Mountain View, Los Gatos, Milpitas, Los Altos. In-home / in-person, plus remote option.

METHOD: reward-based, explicitly no corrections, shock, choke or prong. Will work with families currently using corrective tools provided they're willing to move away from them.

POLICIES TO KNOW: full fee applies on cancellation unless she can fill the slot. Payments non-refundable but transferable to another service at her discretion.

USE THIS FOR: the single highest-leverage purchase — one in-person consult where she watches you walk the dog and calibrates your threshold distance. That's the thing you can't get from a book or a Zoom class.

subtasks.title: Write the week-by-week plan for weeks 1-4
subtasks.description:
DONE — the full four-week plan is written out as the five child subtasks (Week 0 through Week 4). Work them in order; each is self-contained.

THE PLAN IN ONE PARAGRAPH: Week 0 you buy gear and diagnose whether the barking is frustration or fear. Week 1 you stop him rehearsing the behaviour at all, and build the mechanics indoors. Week 2 you take loose-leash walking outside and start counter-conditioning at a distance far enough that he can still eat. Week 3 you upgrade to rewarding him for looking away from other dogs, and start closing distance. Week 4 you run controlled setups with a borrowed calm dog, then measure against your Week 0 baseline and decide whether to continue or escalate.

TIME COMMITMENT: two 5\u201310 minute sessions on weekday evenings, plus one or two longer setup sessions at the weekend. This fits the stated availability. It does not require more than that \u2014 frequency beats duration, and short successful sessions beat long frustrating ones.

THE THREE RULES THAT MATTER MOST:
1. If he won't take a treat, you are too close. Add distance. This is the single most reliable readout you have.
2. Never let pulling work. If the leash goes tight, forward motion stops, every time, no exceptions for "a little" pulling.
3. Change one variable at a time \u2014 distance, or movement, or environment. Never two.

Status is 'waiting' because the plan is written but the weeks themselves are the human's to execute.

subtasks.title: WEEK 0 (this weekend) — Buy equipment and run the frustration-vs-fear assessment
subtasks.description:
Do this before Week 1 starts. Two jobs: gear, and diagnosis.

EQUIPMENT TO BUY (all available at any pet store or online):
- Y-front harness with BOTH a front clip and a top clip. Use the front clip for training walks, the top clip for casual ones. Easy Walk or Balance Harness are the commonly recommended ones.
- 6-foot standard flat leash. NOT retractable — retractables keep constant tension and reinforce pulling.
- 15–30 ft long line, for decompression sniffing walks in open space.
- Optional: head halter (Gentle Leader or Halti) as a backup if the harness isn't enough control. Needs its own gradual introduction — don't just strap it on.
- A treat pouch that clips to your waist. Non-negotiable in practice; fumbling in a pocket loses you the 1-second timing window.
- HIGH VALUE treats: real chicken, cheese, hot dog, freeze-dried liver. Not kibble, not biscuits. Cut to pea size, and prepare far more than feels reasonable — you may feed 15 in a row for a single dog sighting.
- A clicker, or just pick a marker word ("yes!") and use it consistently.

DO NOT BUY: prong collar, choke chain, or e-collar. Per SF SPCA, the dog may stop barking because of the pain, but the risk that he associates the pain with the presence of the other dog is significant, and reactivity can worsen through fear and anxiety. Some dogs are agitated enough to block out the pain and escalate anyway.

THE ASSESSMENT — carry a note on your phone and log every dog sighting for the week:
For each one record: (1) distance when he first noticed, (2) distance when he started barking, (3) body language, (4) how long to recover afterwards, (5) whether he could take a treat.

Score the body language toward one of two columns:
- FRUSTRATED GREETER: loose wiggly body, high fast-wagging tail, whining mixed into the barking, pulls TOWARD the other dog, fine once he actually meets dogs.
- FEAR / DEFENSIVE: hackles up, stiff body, growling, air-snapping, weight back, reacts at very long distances, won't take food, takes minutes to settle.

This single distinction determines how hard the next four weeks will be and whether you need a behaviour consultant rather than a class. It also gives you your starting threshold distance, which every exercise below depends on.

ALSO THIS WEEK: download the free HSSV Reactive Dog Training Guide — https://www.hssv.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Reactive-Dog-Training-Guide-7.11.25.pdf

subtasks.title: WEEK 1 — Stop the rehearsal. Mechanics indoors, management outdoors.
subtasks.description:
GOVERNING IDEA FOR WEEK 1: every walk where he pulls and barks is a rep that makes the behaviour stronger. Week 1 is about stopping the practice, not fixing anything yet. Expect to feel like you're avoiding the problem. You are, deliberately.

MANAGEMENT (all week, every walk):
- Walk at low-traffic times and in low-traffic places. Early morning, late evening, quiet industrial streets, empty school grounds. Accept boring routes.
- The moment you see a dog at distance: cross the street, duck behind a parked car or tree, or turn and go the other way. SF SPCA lists exactly this — avoidance via crossing, ducking behind a car or tree, or a taught 180 turn.
- Goal for the week: ZERO barking episodes. Not fewer. Zero. Every one you dodge is one he doesn't practise.

SKILL 1 — Charge the marker (10 min, day 1–2, indoors)
Say "yes!" then immediately feed a treat. 20 reps. Repeat a few times. He should perk up at the word. This is the foundation of everything else.

SKILL 2 — The emergency U-turn (10 min/day, indoors then quiet street)
Say a cue ("let's go!"), turn 180°, jog 3–4 steps, mark and feed. Make it a fun game, never a yank. Practise until he spins with you happily. This is your escape hatch for the next three years.

SKILL 3 — "Find it" (5 min/day)
Say "find it", toss a treat on the ground. Repeat. Later, this scatter-and-sniff move resets an aroused dog and turns his head away from a trigger. Sniffing is genuinely calming.

SKILL 4 — Loose leash walking, indoors and in the garden only
The rule: reward the loose leash, and a tight leash never works. Only mark, treat, and move forward when the leash is loose. If it goes tight, stop dead — become a tree — and wait for slack, then continue. Never let him get where he wants to go by pulling.
- Mark and treat every 1–2 steps at first as long as he isn't pulling. Yes, that's a lot of treats. The rate drops fast.
- Criteria must be black and white: reward for NO tension. Do not allow "a little" pulling — the dog cannot learn the difference between pulling a little and pulling a lot.
- Feed with your hand at your trouser seam, so the reward position teaches the walking position.
- The visual test: the leash clip hangs straight down, and the leash makes a loose J.

BORDER COLLIE NOTE: add 15 min/day of nosework or a puzzle feeder, and start teaching a trick that has nothing to do with walks. An under-stimulated herding dog is a more reactive dog. Scatter his breakfast in the grass instead of using a bowl.

SESSION LENGTH: 5–10 minutes, twice a day. Short and successful beats long and frustrating.

subtasks.title: WEEK 2 — Loose leash on real pavement + first counter-conditioning at big distance
subtasks.description:
PREREQUISITE: he can walk 10 steps on a loose leash indoors and turns with you on the U-turn cue.

PART 1 — Take loose leash walking outside (15 min, 4–5 evenings)
- Start in the driveway or directly outside the front door, not on a walk. The front door is the most exciting place in his world; treat it as a training location in its own right.
- Same rules: stop when tight, mark and feed at your seam when loose.
- Progress in tiny increments: driveway → 20 metres of pavement → to the end of the street. If he pulls consistently, you've gone somewhere too exciting. Back up.
- SEPARATE THE TWO KINDS OF WALK. A training walk is 15 minutes, front clip, high rate of reinforcement, no distance covered. A sniffing walk is on the long line in an open space where he can just be a dog. Do not try to train on a sniffing walk. He needs both and confusing them ruins both.

PART 2 — Start the Engage-Disengage Game, Level 1 (2–3 sessions this week)
Set up where you can SEE dogs but at a distance he doesn't react at — a bench near a park entrance, a car park overlooking a field. Use your Week 0 log to pick the distance. If in doubt, go further away. Better too far than too close.

LEVEL 1 — reward for LOOKING:
1. At the exact moment he looks at the other dog (ENGAGE), MARK — click or "yes!"
2. Then feed a treat, encouraging him to turn his head to you to take it.
3. A successful rep = he looks at the dog, you mark, he turns back to you for the treat.
4. Repeat. Stay on Level 1 until he's calmly engaging from every direction, especially if the trigger is moving or varying in intensity.

THE THRESHOLD RULE, which matters more than anything else here: the right distance is where he NOTICES the other dog but can still eat and still respond to you. If he won't take a treat, you are too close — that's the single clearest signal in the whole protocol. Per SPCA of Wake County: if he barks and lunges, you went too far too fast — add more distance and repeat. Never wait for him to react before you act.

THE ALTERNATIVE IF HE'S ALREADY STARING: if he locks on before you can mark, switch to the ASPCA approach — as soon as he notices the other dog but before he can overreact, feed treat after treat smoothly and quickly, 10 to 15 in a row, praising calmly. Stop when the dog is gone. This is pure association-building and needs no skill from him.

STOP THE SESSION when treats run out, when he stops eating, or after ~10 minutes. Always end before he's had enough.

STILL AVOIDING: on ordinary walks, keep dodging. Training sessions are the only place you deliberately let him see dogs this week.

subtasks.title: WEEK 3 — Engage-Disengage Level 2, and closing the distance
subtasks.description:
PREREQUISITE: Level 1 is reliable — he looks at a dog and turns straight back to you for the treat, repeatedly, calmly.

LEVEL 2 — reward for LOOKING AWAY (start at the SAME distance Level 1 worked at, do not move closer yet):
1. Let him notice the other dog.
2. Wait 3–5 seconds to see whether he disengages and looks away on his own.
3. The precise moment he looks away — MARK. Then feed.
4. If he fixates for longer than 5 seconds, go back to Level 1.
5. If he reacts, or doesn't turn back to you after the mark, move further away and reset at an easier distance.
Aim for a run of successful reps before changing anything. Karen Pryor's guidance is to succeed consistently at Level 2 before progressing.

CLOSING DISTANCE — the rule for the whole rest of this process:
Change ONE variable at a time. Distance, or the other dog's movement, or the environment. Never two.
Move closer only in small steps, and only after a run of clean reps at the current distance. Per SPCA of Wake County: when he looks up at you for more, go closer and repeat — and if he barks and lunges, you went too far too fast, so add distance and repeat.
Expect to go backwards on some days. A dog who did brilliantly on Tuesday can fall apart on Thursday because he slept badly or a bin lorry went past. That's normal and not failure.

ADD THIS WEEK — the pattern of the real walk:
Start using the U-turn and "find it" mid-walk on actual dog sightings, rather than only in set-up sessions. Sequence when a dog appears at distance:
1. Spot it early — this is your job, scan ahead constantly.
2. Create distance — cross, or step behind a car.
3. Mark and feed while it passes, or run engage-disengage if he's under threshold.
4. Move on calmly. Don't linger to "prove" anything.

LOOSE LEASH: by now you should be getting a loose J on a quiet street for most of a 15-minute training walk. Start adding mild distractions — a cat across the road, a jogger — while keeping the pulling criteria absolutely consistent.

DO NOT DO THIS: do not let him greet other dogs on leash as a reward. Best Friends cautions that on-leash greetings carry risk, because frustration buildup can lead to a scuffle. On-leash greeting also keeps the "other dogs mean something happens" association alive, which is what you're trying to dismantle.

subtasks.title: WEEK 4 — Controlled setups with a real decoy dog, then review the month
subtasks.description:
This is the week that needs another person, which is exactly why a class or a trainer earns its money here.

THE SET-UP SESSION (2 this week):
Recruit a friend with a calm, well-mannered, non-reactive dog on leash — Best Friends describes exactly this arrangement, a helper with a steady dog. A neighbour's placid older dog is ideal. Ask nicely; offer coffee.
- Start at a distance well beyond your current working threshold, in a big open space, not a narrow path.
- Run engage-disengage Level 2 with the helper's dog standing still.
- Then change ONE thing: the helper's dog walks slowly parallel to you, still at distance. Reward for calm.
- Then, over multiple sessions, gradually reduce distance.
- Best Friends' technique also uses the dog's own desired outcome — moving away from what's bothering him — as the reinforcer for an alternative behaviour. So: he looks calmly at the decoy, you mark, and you walk away from it. Relief itself becomes the payment. This is powerful for a fear-based dog.
- Keep sessions under 10 minutes. Stop while it's still going well.

IF YOU ENROLLED IN A CLASS: this is roughly where a structured course starts putting you in a controlled group setting with other reactive dogs at managed distances. You'll have decoy dogs supplied and a trainer watching your timing, which is the part that's hard to self-assess.

END-OF-MONTH REVIEW — compare against your Week 0 log:
1. At what distance does he now first bark? Bigger number than Week 0 = it's working.
2. Can he take food closer to a dog than he could in Week 0?
3. How fast does he recover after a reaction?
4. Roughly how many reactions per walk, vs Week 0?
5. Is he walking on a loose leash on a quiet street?
Progress here is measured in metres of threshold distance and seconds of recovery time, not in the dog being "cured." A month is enough to see a clear trend, not enough to finish.

DECISION POINT AT THE END OF WEEK 4:
- CLEAR IMPROVEMENT → carry on for another 4–8 weeks, same method, keep shrinking distance. Consider an in-person class to get real-world practice.
- FLAT, OR WORSE → stop self-directing and book a professional. Sniffspot's guidance is that if progress stalls, if reactivity worsens despite consistent work, or if you're not confident you're reading your dog correctly, bring in a professional — a certified trainer with reactivity experience catches what you'll miss.
- ANY GROWLING, SNAPPING, OR BITE ATTEMPT → stop the DIY work now and get a CDBC/CBCC-KA behaviour consultant. Note that most reactive-dog classes exclude dogs with a bite history, so this narrows your options and you should act early.

WHAT WEEK 5+ LOOKS LIKE: same protocol, more environments, shorter distances, plus a real outlet for the herding drive — scent work, rally, or urban parkour. HSSV's Top Dogs Level 3 is built on exactly that idea, continuing counter-conditioning through a sport so the dog gets calmer around dogs while learning something fun.

subtasks.title: DECIDE: which trainer option (or none) — 15 min, do this first
subtasks.description:
Everything else waits on this. Read the report and the three OPTION subtasks, then pick one:

- A) HSSV Top Dogs Level 1 — $300, online, Wed 6:15pm, starts 19 Aug 2026
- B) In Tune / Nancy Le — $195–325 initial consult, in person at your house
- C) D For Dogz Growly Dog Foundations — $595, Sat 9:30am + Wed 6:30pm, Palo Alto
- A + B combined — the recommendation, roughly $500–625
- None — run the four-week plan solo and reassess at the end of Week 4

There is no wrong answer here that can't be corrected in a month. The four-week plan runs identically either way, so a delay in deciding costs you nothing except the 19 Aug cohort. What you're really buying with a trainer is a calibrated eye on your threshold distance and access to decoy dogs.

BUDGET REALITY CHECK: this problem is worth spending on at 14 months, when it's still cheap to fix. It gets more expensive — in money and in the dog's quality of life — the longer it's rehearsed.

subtasks.title: Email Nancy Le to book an initial consult and confirm evening/weekend availability
subtasks.description:
ONLY IF you picked Option B or A+B.

Email: Nancy@Intunedogtraining.com
Booking page: https://www.intunedogtraining.com/book
No phone number is published — email or the web form is the way in.

WHAT TO SAY: 14-month-old rescue border collie mix. Pulls hard on leash, barks and lunges at other dogs on walks. No bite history. Looking for an initial consultation focused on leash reactivity, specifically to have someone watch your handling and calibrate your threshold distance.

ASK SPECIFICALLY:
1. Evening and weekend availability — an older version of her site listed consults on Thursdays and Fridays only, so confirm this works before committing. This is the one open question on this option.
2. Confirm the fee for your case — the published range is $195–$325 for the initial consult, $130–$215 for follow-ups.
3. Tiered pricing if your household earns under $115K/year: https://www.intunedogtraining.com/booktier
4. Whether she'd recommend one calibration session alongside a group class, rather than her standard 6-session arc — that's the cheaper hybrid and worth asking about directly.

NOTE HER POLICY: full fee applies if you cancel and she can't fill the slot. Payments non-refundable, though transferable at her discretion. Put the appointment in your calendar properly.

subtasks.title: Buy the walking kit this weekend
subtasks.description:
Do this regardless of the trainer decision — nothing in the four-week plan works without it, and the plan starts Monday.

SHOPPING LIST:
- Y-front harness with both front and top clip (Easy Walk or Balance Harness)
- 6 ft flat leash — NOT retractable
- 15–30 ft long line for sniffing walks
- Treat pouch that clips to your waist
- High-value treats: chicken, cheese, hot dog or freeze-dried liver, cut to pea size. Buy more than seems sensible.
- Clicker (optional — a consistent marker word works)

DO NOT BUY prong, choke or e-collars. They risk making dog-directed reactivity worse rather than better by pairing discomfort with the sight of other dogs.

Available at any pet store or online; nothing here is specialist.
